newsitem.title: PERU: Peru privatization to get second wind in late '97.
newsitem.headline: Peru privatization to get second wind in late '97.

text.p: Peru's privatization program is going to get a second wind in late 1997 with renewed efforts to get railway, mining and oil assets under private control later this year.
The head of government privatization board COPRI announced plans to privatize Peru's rail network in the fourth quarter.
"The railways will be (privatized) in three stages, as three companies. Probably in October or November," Ernesto Mitsumasu, executive director of COPRI since April, told foreign journalists.
State rail company Enafer SA has an estimated 1,000 miles (1,500 km) of track throughout Peru. Mitsumasu would not give state estimates of the value of those assets.
The COPRI head confirmed the government's plans to relaunch its program to place state oil assets under the control of private firms by auctioning eight concessions to operate oil terminals.

Offering concessions in the oil sector marks a change in government strategy, which had previously passed state firm Petroperu's non-exploration oil assets into the private sector with direct sales. The auction of the concessions is slated for the third quarter.
Last November, the government put on hold its oil privatization program after the sale of a 60 percent stake in its La Pampilla refinery raised public fears of gasoline price hikes.
Mitsumasu hailed the April 18 privatization of the huge metallurgic complex La Oroya -- Peru's last major sell-off -- as a "great success."
He said La Oroya's new majority holder, Mexico's Industriales Peoles SA, would decide by June 30 whether to also purchase the state's remaining 49 percent.

The government's privatization program has drawn since May 1992 direct income of $7.095 billion and has also brought commitments from buyers to invest $7.50 billion, according to latest COPRI figures.

But with few major assets left to sell, the government has said it will now concentrate on granting concessions to carry out public sector infrastructure projects. The government hopes to attract $8 billion in this so-called "second phase" of the privatization program.

"If Peoles does not buy this portion, it could possibly enter the citizens' participation plan," he said, referring to the government's Citizens' Participation in Privatization program intended to involve individual, small investors in the sell-off process through stock placements.

Peoles became the majority owner of the complex with an $185 million offer, and could buy out the government completely by offering a further $192.6 million, state miner Centromin has said. La Oroya's workers, however, have preferential rights to buy ten percent of the mixed company.
The government's next mining sale is Centromin's Mahr Tunel company, which runs the San Cristobal and Andaychagua mines, on June 20.

A month later, Peru's second state miner Minero Peru is set to auction the rights to its copper-rich Michiquillay deposit, which has already attracted strong interest from seven U.S., Japanese and Canadian firms.

With a string of sales also slated in the fishing, water and agriculture sectors -- and plans being laid to sell state packages in electric utility Edegel and Banco Continental -- a complete new privatization timetable is due to be issued next week, Mitsumasu added.
